title: MongoDB Named a Leader in Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems 2026
summary:
I’m thrilled to share that MongoDB has been named a Leader in the new Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems.

We believe our placement as a Leader in a brand-new category reflects the investments MongoDB has made in our data platform and the strength of our product offerings. We also believe it reflects the trust our more than 70,000 customers, including ~75% of the Fortune 100, have placed in MongoDB.

Agents are changing what an operational database has to do: absorb spiky demand, keep context fresh, and keep cost per task down. Here’s how we see MongoDB doing that, and what it means for your next architecture decision.

What is the operational database category?

This year, the former Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Database Management Systems has been split into separate Magic Quadrant reports for Operational Database and Lakehouse, because we believe the buying criteria and decision-makers associated with each differ. If you’re choosing the database that runs your apps and agents, you now have a report written for that decision.

Gartner defines the market for cloud operational database management systems (DBMS) as software designed to store and manipulate data and delivered primarily as platform as a service (PaaS) in the cloud. These systems primarily optimize routine business transactions, data writes, and application state management. They prioritize high concurrency and low latency while enforcing transactional guarantees to ensure data integrity.¹

Put plainly, these systems power the services that the world depends on, from healthcare and telecommunications to card payments and banking, to retail solutions that touch millions of people.

Why your data platform is important to AI success

I traveled a lot in 2026, meeting with scores of MongoDB customers and partners across dozens of cities (in multiple countries!). One theme kept coming up: the data platform decides whether AI works. A few threads connect what I’ve been hearing:

  • Agents make demand spikier. Where a person might click a button or two to accomplish a task, an agent will make dozens of calls (and might even spawn other agents). That's why elasticity matters more than another point of peak throughput.

  • Cost per task, not cost per token or cost per seat, is what organizations looking to control AI spending should focus on. As my colleague Pete Johnson has written, the goal of every org should be spending the right 200K tokens instead of the wrong million. When your operational data, vector search, and reranking live in the same platform, you can filter, retrieve, and rerank in one pipeline—saving money and improving results.

  • One data foundation is simpler to run. Teams build AI applications directly on MongoDB’s intelligent data platform instead of governing separate components. As Jacky Koh, Co-founder of Relevance AI, put it, “Having both the operational and vector database in the same platform makes managing scale much simpler and managing performance much more effective.”

In our opinion, AI success depends on having the right data platform. MongoDB combines a state-of-the-art operational database with search, vector search, hybrid search, and built-in embedding models that keep context fresh (giving agents the information they need to act reliably). MongoDB also gives customers the freedom to run anywhere, helping them move quickly today while enabling them to change deployment postures later.

How MongoDB enables (AI) innovation

2026 was another big year for MongoDB. Everything we do aims to help organizations move faster, build smarter, and to simplify complex architectures, and 2026 was no different.

The product releases and capabilities we shared this year reinforce the importance of data to AI success, and underscore how MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era. Here are some highlights:

  • MongoDB 9.0 

    • 9.0 is the fastest, most performant version of MongoDB we’ve ever built, and it’s designed for applications and agents that act on live data. Compared to MongoDB 8.0, transactional workloads in 9.0 achieve up to 20% higher throughput, enabling applications to process more business-critical operations more efficiently. Find-one queries are up to 35% faster, and update-one queries are up to 30% faster. That means more users, transactions, and AI activity before you add infrastructure or re-architect applications. Also now generally available as part of MongoDB 9.0 are Intelligent Workload Management, expanded Queryable Encryption capabilities, and the MongoDB Extension for Hibernate ORM.

  • Atlas Infinite 

    • Atlas Infinite is the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. It was built for the reality of the agentic era, when demand is constant, unpredictable, and extreme. It absorbs bursts of traffic and scales from prototype to petabyte on the same high-performance foundation, so organizations never outgrow it.

  • Atlas Agent Engine

    • Atlas Agent Engine lets developers build, deploy, and govern agents with persistent memory, context, built-in guardrails, and state management. Teams move from prototype to production without stitching together custom state stores, guardrails, and data pipelines.

  • New Voyage AI models and capabilities

    • Voyage AI by MongoDB embedding models and rerankers run next to your operational data, so agents retrieve accurate context in one pipeline instead of several. Recent Voyage AI releases include the Rerank 3 series, voyage-code-4, a retrieval model tuned specifically for coding agents, and automated embedding in Atlas Vector Search.

And that only scratches the surface; for everything MongoDB has released, and for the latest product news and ways we’ve innovated on behalf of customers, see our What’s New page.

Building (for) the road ahead

To paraphrase MongoDB CEO Dev Ittycheria, we expect that the data layer will eventually become an integral part of every organization’s control plane. As software moves from systems of record to systems that act on their own, the data layer of the tech stack will become ever more important.

The customers I’ve been meeting say they no longer want software that explains what happened. They need software, and the technology they rely on, to keep pace with what's happening right now. MongoDB was built for this reality, and we can’t wait to see what’s next.

title: AI Demand is Constant, Unpredictable, and Extreme. MongoDB is Built for It.
summary:
When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers. Diners feel it when they try to get a reservation at a trendy restaurant that’s fully booked for months. Websites and applications feel it when they go viral and get an accidental DDoS from a “Reddit Hug of Death.”

Unpredictable spikes in demand are only becoming more common, and scaling resources to meet them is hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen big shifts in the amount of demand systems need to handle. First, the internet era, then the cloud era, we saw increased demand that was often predictable. Think of an annual flash sale or regular seasonality. Things might speed up, with more frequent spikes, but they were still spikes you could plan around.

Then AI happened. And this is where we live now: demand that’s constant, unpredictable, and extreme, increasing in frequency and intensity at the same time. If the internet era taught customers to expect an instant response, then the AI era is teaching them to expect something else: instant value. You can snap a photo of something you want, and an agent can identify it, buy it, and have it on your doorstep tomorrow. Those capabilities cut both ways. Change now hits every layer underneath faster and harder than before. The user isn't only human anymore. Agents are in the product too.

Agents don’t ease in. The second they’re on, they hit your system with massive, simultaneous reads and writes. They also take in and act on more information at once than any team of people ever could. Enterprises need a data layer built for that reality, where the only predictable thing is how unpredictable the load will be. Teams that can scale into those spikes will be the ones that last.

Introducing Atlas Infinite

Today, we're announcing Atlas Infinite, the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. Atlas Infinite is purpose-built to handle the speed of development and unpredictable demand of applications that customers expect, with independent scaling of compute and storage to absorb sudden bursts of traffic.

Atlas Infinite is not a new database. It's a new deployment option within Atlas. Same document model, same drivers and APIs, no code changes required. Also, the current deployment option you know and love as MongoDB Atlas is not going anywhere. It just has a new name, MongoDB Atlas Core. Atlas Core and Atlas Infinite are the two database deployment options within the Atlas platform. You pick the right one for each workload.

How does Atlas Infinite deal with four key scaling and future-proofing problems organizations are dealing with today?

  1. Scaling delay: Gone. Atlas Infinite cuts read scaling time by more than 96% compared to Atlas Core. Compute and storage automatically scale independently within minutes, not hours.

  2. Storage ceiling: 10x higher. Atlas Infinite grows with you, from prototype to a petabyte, on the same foundation. You scale on your terms, when you need more performance, not when you run out of room. Atlas Infinite supports replica sets that hold 10x the data of replica sets in Atlas Core. 

  3. Capacity planning: No more guesswork. Atlas Infinite meets your needs in real time as you scale up and down. Atlas Infinite also runs more efficiently on the same hardware compared to Atlas Core, so you get nearly triple the performance per dollar.

  4. Re-architecture: Not required. Zero application changes required. Enjoy more elasticity and scalability on literally the same database.

This isn't only a scalability story. It's a more capable, more performant engine. Internal tests* using MongoDB 9.0 have shown that Atlas Infinite provides 189% more throughput per dollar compared with Atlas Core. And customers like Icon Solutions are using it to drive more growth.

"Atlas Infinite let us process 55% more transactions per second than our equivalent previous setup on MongoDB 8.0, with zero application changes. In payments, that kind of headroom without a re-architecture means faster, more reliable experiences for the customers on the other end of every transaction," said Mike Wallis, Head of DevOps at Icon Solutions.

Atlas Infinite is available as a public preview, and I can’t wait for you to try out the next generation of MongoDB Atlas.

MongoDB 9.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

In addition, we just released the best version of MongoDB ever, MongoDB 9.0. We’ve hardened the core to ensure a rock-solid foundation for the most demanding enterprises, and we’re setting a new bar for security, durability, availability, and performance.

That bar was already high. MongoDB 8.0 was released just two years ago, and today, nearly 80% of our Atlas fleet has adopted it, with higher customer satisfaction and stronger retention among these customers.

We are proud of what 8.0 delivered, and 9.0 pushes further still. Here are some of my favorite enhancements in MongoDB 9.0.

Performance*: 

  • In our internal tests against MongoDB 8.0, MongoDB 9.0 delivers:

    • Up to 35% faster find-one queries

    • Up to 30% faster update-one queries

    • Up to 2x throughput on large instances

    • Up to 20% higher throughput for transactional workloads

Security:

  • Queryable Encryption now supports prefix, suffix, and substring searches, allowing organizations to query sensitive information without ever decrypting it. 

  • Expanded private networking capabilities make it easier to deploy MongoDB Atlas securely across complex enterprise environments.

Durability and Availability:

  • Intelligent Workload Management automatically protects clusters when they are overloaded with requests and ensures short-running operations continue when demand is unpredictable.

  • Enhanced backup, restore, and recovery capabilities help organizations to maintain application availability and speed recovery when disruptions occur.

Observability & Developer Productivity:

  • Expanded observability into application and database performance

  • New developer productivity features that make it easier to modernize applications with familiar tools and frameworks, without costly rewrites.

MongoDB 9.0 continues to give you the freedom to run anywhere. MongoDB 9.0 is available in MongoDB Atlas and in self-managed environments through MongoDB Enterprise Advanced and MongoDB Community Edition.

MongoDB 9.0 on Atlas Infinite changes the calculus on scale. It's not something you plan around anymore, it's just there when you need it. There's never been a better time to build on MongoDB.

*Performance results are based on internal MongoDB testing comparing MongoDB 9.0 and MongoDB 8.0 using public benchmark methodologies. Results may vary by workload, deployment, hardware, and configuration.

title: Agentic Treasury: How AI Agents Turn Cash Blind Spots Into Real-Time, Governed Action
summary:
At 8 a.m., a $4 million payroll is due, but an expected customer payment hasn’t arrived. Leafy International’s treasury agent spots the gap in live payment data. It checks current balances and recommends a cash sweep from an overnight deposit. It’s enough to fund payroll while keeping Leafy’s $1 million minimum cash buffer intact.

Just as the treasurer reviews the proposal, an approved, time-stamped market feed flags a material EUR/USD move after a central bank announcement. The agent connects the signal to Leafy’s upcoming euro payment, refreshes the exposure, and flags it for review. A market alert is a reason to reassess, not permission to trade.

The treasurer views the rationale, data source, and update time, and then approves or delegates within the agreed mandate. If a balance, payment status, or foreign exchange (FX) rate changes before execution, the agent checks again. This is agentic treasury: Monitoring relevant conditions, recommending next steps, and helping carry them out only when authorized.

Leafy International is fictional, but the pressures and actions are real. Treasury teams are exploring how AI can improve decisions across payments, cash, working capital, and financial risk—and how to govern these systems.

Agentic treasury has two key requirements:

  • Context that stays current as balances, payments, and markets move

  • An independent check that confirms each action is authorized before it runs.

MongoDB provides the data layer for both, keeping the agent's context fresh as conditions change, and holding the controls and audit log that decide what the agent is allowed to do.

The industry shift to AI action

Cash and liquidity optimization remain persistent challenges for treasury teams. Nearly two-thirds of people surveyed by AFP cite cash management and forecasting as a top priority, while nearly 50% say they’re concerned about liquidity and cash planning. For the first time, AI and automation also ranked among the top five priorities, cited by 30% of respondents.

Similarly, Citi’s 2026 MEA treasury survey highlights that half of those surveyed point to cash visibility and forecasting and liquidity optimization as their biggest concerns.

Interest is already turning into practice. According to Strategic Treasurer's 2025 AI in Treasury & Finance Survey, 22% of companies already use agentic AI, with 18% reporting active use within their own treasury or finance department. Beyond current use, 25% are actively testing agentic tools, 32% have experimented with them, and 72% say they understand the technology.

Adoption is early, but agentic AI is no longer hypothetical. The opportunity lies in delivering timely, consolidated context that surfaces liquidity gaps earlier. This frees treasurers to focus on judgment and exceptions rather than monitoring out-of-date dashboards.

From batch snapshots to continuous operations

Traditional treasury workflows rely on batch processing of morning balance files and end-of-day reporting. This lag exposes teams to intraday liquidity risks and unhedged FX volatility. A continuous, real-time view of cash positioning and market data enables proactive liquidity management and dynamic risk mitigation.

Treasury agents need current, decision-ready context across authorized balances, payment and receipt status, deposit terms, FX rates, and relevant events. Not every signal update calls for action. The agents reassess only when a material signal could change a decision. Freshness should match urgency since payroll cutoffs need tighter checks than overnight-surplus reviews.

A continuous operating model runs on a repeatable loop:

  1. Sense: Gather the current context (e.g., authorized balances, payment and receipt status, market signals) with each source and update time visible.

  2. Plan: Compare the projected cash position with what must be funded, such as payroll and the required buffer. Identify any surplus available to deploy.

  3. Propose: Explain a specific action, its rationale, and its expected effect on cash or exposure.

  4. Check and act: Confirm that the action is authorized and the data is fresh enough for the decision’s urgency. Then execute, request approval, or stop.

The contextual layer: 4 data capabilities an agent needs

An agent is only as trustworthy as its context: balances, payments, market signals, policy, and memory, each with its source and age visible. Four data capabilities keep that context current and useful.

1. Detect relevant changes

Relevant events can include an overdue payment, a payment-status change, or an authorized FX or news feed. After the application ingests an external update into MongoDB, change streams can notify an agent of the change. The agent then refreshes its context and reassesses. Atlas Database Triggers build on change streams and automatically run a function when a matching change occurs, such as a payment-status update.

2. Absorb new shapes of information

Suppose an ISO 20022 feed adds a remittancePurpose field. Teams can validate and map it without reshaping historical payment information. MongoDB’s flexible document model lets new payments include the field while older ones retain their shape.

With schema validation, teams can require the remittancePurpose field on every new payment and block writes that break the rules at the database level. Validation levels and actions control how strictly those rules apply, so teams can roll out enforcement gradually without rewriting historical payments.

3. Retrieve by meaning, not just keywords

Explaining a recommendation may require market events, FX trends, invoice or remittance details, and the policy governing the decision. MongoDB Vector Search retrieves by semantic meaning and can rank candidates by relevance. Automated Embedding generates embeddings inside MongoDB, reducing the need for a separate pipeline. Keeping context alongside balances and payments helps connect relevant evidence to a decision.

4. Remember with agent memory

Short-term memory tracks the current payroll run, balances, and pending approvals. Long-term memory preserves reusable context, such as payroll calendars and target buffers. Time-sensitive details can expire while useful context carries forward. Proposed actions, checks, and outcomes remain in the audit log. These are among the approaches for managing agent memory with MongoDB.

Make delegation safe by design

Dependable agentic treasury requires decision-ready context and an independent, governed check before action. Timely data does not authorize action.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) offers what law firm Ashurst Perkins Coie calls the first reference framework of its kind for governing AI agents in financial services at runtime. It is not a regulatory compliance checklist.

In this framework, the agent submits a governance envelope containing the proposed action, its action trace, and relevant context. Four components work through that envelope:

  • Agent identity: Verifies the registered agent.

  • Controls repository: Supplies the policy, regulatory, and delegated-authority controls that the disposition engine applies.

  • Disposition engine: Evaluates each proposal against those controls and decides the outcome.

  • Audit log: Keeps a tamper-evident, append-only record of the envelope, mandate, checks, and outcome.

In the cash sweep example, the agent first assembles the context it needs: its authority, the deposit terms, the current balance, pending payments, and the freshness of the data. If a material input is stale, the agent refreshes it or pauses before submitting the action for governance. The check returns one of four outcomes:

  • Auto-execute: The action is routine, within mandate, and passes all checks.

  • Observe: The action proceeds, but is flagged for monitoring and later review.

  • Escalate: The action may be appropriate, but needs an authorized approver.

  • Deny: The action conflicts with a hard limit, customer instruction, or restriction.

Governance data also varies in shape. Policies, delegated-authority limits, action traces, and check results differ by product, jurisdiction, and mandate. This variety suits MongoDB’s flexible document model.

An FX hedge and a cash sweep, for example, have different structures yet both belong in the same governance envelope. A document can take the shape each action needs and can change as execution unfolds. No rigid, predefined table design is required.

title: Build Once, Grow Freely: Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite
summary:
Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run.

In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls.

MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together.

How Atlas Infinite works

A new deployment option within MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Infinite separates compute from storage so each scales independently and rapidly. Storage moves into a fully managed layer that handles replication, durability, and backup across availability zones, so compute no longer has to carry the data with it.

The impact is dramatic. Read replicas come online in minutes because there's no data to copy. A single shard holds up to 128 TB, so you no longer shard just to add disk space. You only pay for the data you store, not capacity provisioned in advance, so a small team never has to buy a bigger compute tier just to get more disk. And it’s all driven by the same MongoDB API, drivers, and tooling, so your application doesn’t need to change.

The separation of storage and compute matters most where agentic applications grow fastest: the retrieval layer. Every answer an assistant gives and every step an agent takes starts with a search over your data, and the data behind that search, especially vector embeddings, can grow large quickly. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search running natively on Atlas Infinite, that data lives on the same foundation as the rest of your application and can grow without re-architecture. Build your agentic workload once and keep scaling it on the same foundation as demand grows.

Figure 1. Compute and storage as independent layers in Atlas Infinite.

Retrieval, built into the database

Many retrieval stacks are cobbled together from disconnected components—a database, a search engine, and a vector database—which means running all of those separate parts, plus managing the pipelines that keep everything in sync. On Atlas Infinite, retrieval is part of the platform, so there are fewer pieces to build, secure, and maintain. Here is what that looks like:

  • One platform, nothing to stitch together: On Atlas Infinite, your database and retrieval work together seamlessly, with no separate search engine or vector database to stand up, sync, or monitor. MongoDB Atlas keeps your indexes in sync with your data automatically, so there is no pipeline for your team to build or maintain, and no extra systems to copy sensitive data into or secure. With Atlas Infinite, retrieval is built in, alongside the ability to scale to absorb unpredictable demand with zero waste.
  • Start small, never outgrow your data platform: A team can start with a 5GB prototype that includes semantic search and keep building on the same foundation. Rather than sizing and maintaining two infrastructures, storage grows automatically with your data, billed only for what you store. The operational data behind your search has room to grow to petabyte scale on Atlas Infinite, with no re-platforming when the application takes off.
  • Agent memory and context retrieval: Give agents one place to store and retrieve context, history, and state alongside your operational data. Support thousands of agents hitting your retrieval layer while also persisting agent memory and context within a single, durable system that scales when they need it.

Figure 2. Search and Vector Search run alongside the database on Atlas Infinite, with indexes kept in sync automatically and data stored once in Atlas-managed storage.

How Atlas Infinite handles your largest text and vector workloads

Separating compute from storage in the database also changes the scaling behavior and economics of large retrieval workloads. Text and vector data lives in the database first, where it drives storage requirements. Because Atlas Infinite manages that storage separately from compute, the economics come down to one property of the data: how well it compresses.

Databases shrink data on disk with compression, which works by finding repetition. Text is full of repetition: common words, repeated field names, predictable structure. Text in MongoDB typically compresses to about 40% of its original size. An embedding is an array of decimal values with almost no repetition, so it shrinks by only about 13%. In practice, a vector takes up as much space on disk as it does in your application.

How each deployment option stores that data

Atlas Core uses attached storage volumes. Each node in a replica set keeps a full copy of the data on its own disk, provisioned ahead of time with room to grow, and compute and storage come in matched tiers. That gives every node complete isolation and predictable performance, and it's the right fit for many workloads, especially ones where data and query load grow together.

Vector workloads tend to be storage-driven because high-dimension embeddings are so large. A RAG knowledge base can hold hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings, which drives up storage needs relative to query volume. On Atlas Core, storage can drive scaling decisions: once you outgrow a tier’s maximum disk size, you have to move up a tier to get more storage, even if you don’t need more compute, and very large datasets eventually call for sharding.

On Atlas Infinite, compute and storage scale independently. Storage is billed per logical (uncompressed) GB of data you store, metered hourly. Replication across availability zones happens inside the storage layer and isn't billed separately. There's no headroom to provision, and because a shard holds up to 128 TB, a growing dataset doesn't push you to a larger compute tier or to more shards. Because embeddings barely compress, their logical size and their size on disk are nearly the same, so you pay only for the data you store and nothing for the copies and headroom underneath it. As vector collections grow to hundreds of millions of documents, that billing model becomes an advantage.

Here is an example. For a collection with 100 million documents, each with a 1,024-dimension float32 embedding and about 1 KB of other fields, storage is roughly 500 GB uncompressed.  Assuming moderate query traffic, an M30 cluster tier’s compute is sufficient.

On Atlas Core, since embeddings barely compress, the data shrinks to ~435GB on disk. Each node also needs space for the oplog and room for the collection to grow. At 1.3× headroom, that comes to about 565 GB per node, more than the 512 GB an M30 supports, so the cluster has to move up to an M40 for the disk. On Atlas Infinite, the cluster stays at the compute tier its queries need, and storage is billed once on the 500 GB it holds. With storage billed once and no tier-up for disk, the total monthly cost of this deployment, Search Nodes included, comes out about 25% lower than on Core. At 1 billion vectors (about 5 TB), it is about 30% lower, and the gap keeps widening as vector data grows. These figures are modeled on list prices in US East, with Search Nodes sized to the smallest tier that fits the index, so your results will vary.

Where the difference is smaller

Text-heavy search workloads also see a TCO benefit on Atlas Infinite, around 5% to 10% cost reduction at multi-terabyte scale. Text compresses well, so Core's storage cost per GB is already low. The advantage of Atlas Infinite comes from deferring early tier-ups and delaying sharding for disk. Under 500 GB, the two deployment options are roughly even on cost, so a smaller workload gets Atlas Infinite’s room to grow without paying more for it. Choose the deployment option based on the elasticity and growth you expect.

Get started with Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite

MongoDB Search and Vector Search are available on Atlas Infinite in public preview on AWS. Choose Atlas Infinite as the deployment option for your next workload, add a search index the way you would on Atlas Core, and keep building on the same foundation as your application grows. Whether you’re prototyping an AI feature or running a large production application, you can start small and keep going. Start with the Atlas Infinite documentation.

title: MongoDB Acquires Firebolt to Bring Lightning-Fast Real-Time Analytics Into Its Intelligent Data Platform
summary:
Real-time analytics on live operational data, built so applications and AI agents can act on what’s happening now.

The most valuable analytics no longer live in a dashboard. They live inside the application. A logistics app reroutes a shipment around a delay. A retail system reorders inventory before the shelf goes empty. A payments platform flags unusual behavior before the transaction clears.

Each of these decisions requires comparing live operational data against historical patterns. Which routes are backing up, and is that normal? What’s selling faster than usual, and should we restock? Is this login typical for this account at this time of day? Enterprises that can answer these questions in the moment adapt as conditions change. Those that can’t are reacting to yesterday.

Data infrastructure has long been split into two worlds: operational databases that run applications, and data warehouses that analyze what already happened. That paradigm was built for humans looking at morning dashboards, where data a few hours or days old was fine. As analytics moved into applications, real-time analytics emerged as a category of its own, combining complex queries over massive datasets with the speed, freshness, and concurrency that live applications demand. Agents raise the bar on all three. They act continuously, can drive thousands of concurrent queries, and need sub-second answers on fresh data. As businesses rely more on agents, real-time analytics becomes a core part of their data infrastructure.

Eliminate the data-movement tax

Running analytics on operational data often means copying it into a separate system, forcing organizations to build and maintain data pipelines, keep systems in sync, and run yet another platform. Even once the data is flowing, the added complexity, operational overhead, infrastructure cost, and risk of stale answers remain. This is the data-movement tax, and it compounds as agents drive more decisions.

Systems that require customers to move and synchronize data across separate platforms often struggle to deliver fresh answers at the speed and scale that live applications need. For MongoDB customers, the operational data their applications and agents rely on is already in MongoDB, so analytics should be able to run there too, at the source. That's why MongoDB acquired Firebolt.

One platform for operational data and real-time analytics

By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB’s Intelligent Data Platform, we’re bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt’s engine will run right alongside your database, and we’ll keep it in sync automatically, so there’s no pipeline to build or manage. You’ll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure.

Our Intelligent Data Platform already brings together operational data, search and vector search, Voyage AI models, stream processing, and the ability to build and run agents in production. Real-time analytics will extend that foundation, enabling applications and agents to analyze live data and act on it in the moment. Over time, customers will also be able to analyze data from other sources and formats alongside their MongoDB data.

When analytics powers a live application, an outage no longer just delays a report. It breaks the customer experience or stalls an agent mid-decision. MongoDB operates in this mission-critical world: today, approximately 75% of the Fortune 100 trust MongoDB with applications that require the highest levels of security, durability, and availability. We’re bringing that same level of reliability and operational excellence to real-time analytics.

Why Firebolt, and what’s next

Firebolt’s analytics engine is proven in production. It was built from the start for the high concurrency required by live applications and agents, not just internal dashboards and reports. title: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables
summary:
Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts.

Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife(1) rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers.

That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one.

One rule drives everything

A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram into this new shape. That’s the wrong instinct.

The core idea is to model the data around what the business does with it, not around how the entities look on a diagram. Concretely, that means designing for the policy lifecycle (quote, underwrite, issue, bill, endorse, renew, cancel, claim) and asking, at each step, what gets read and written together.

Once you ask that question, every design choice reduces to one decision: whether to embed or reference.

Embed or reference: The decision that matters

For any two related pieces of data, you have two options. Embed one inside the other, so they live in a single document. Or reference one from the other, storing just an identifier that points to a separate document, the way a relational foreign key does.

The test can be reduced to two very simple statements:

  • Embed data that is part of something and is always read alongside it.

  • Reference data that has its own lifecycle or is shared across many records.

Apply that to a policy and the answers fall out naturally. Coverages belong inside the policy. Nobody ever looks up collision coverage without the policy it sits within. The insured vehicle belongs inside the policy—as does the event history, because an endorsement or a cancellation is meaningless apart from the contract it changed. In document form, that looks like this:

Anyone in the business can read that. It looks like the policy.

The claim follows the same logic, with a payoff that finance teams will appreciate. A claim’s reserves and payments belong inside the claim document. Because a single document is always written atomically, posting a reserve and updating the claim’s total becomes one operation that either fully succeeds or doesn’t happen at all. There’s no window where the ledger and the claim disagree.

Now let’s look at the other side of the test. A customer’s policies should not be embedded inside the customer record. Policies are large, they change constantly, and they’re almost always looked up by policy number rather than through the customer record. Instead, store policies in their own collection and have each policy reference its customer by ID. Claims should not be embedded inside policies either, because a claim can outlive the policy that spawned it: a canceled policy can still have open claims. Store claims separately, with each claim referencing the policy it belongs to.

The agent who sold the policy and the product it was written on should also be referenced, not embedded, and here the reasoning is operational. Thousands of policies share one agent and one product. Embed the agent’s details, and a change to their license number becomes a write across every policy in their book. Keep the product catalog as the single, versioned source of truth, and let the policy store only a point-in-time snapshot of the coverage terms it was bound against.

Two storms that test the design

Insurance also stress-tests data models in a way few other industries do: catastrophes.

The hurricane claim

Most auto and property claims carry fewer than 10 supporting attachments (photos, estimates, or a police report, for example). Embedding them in the claim is fine. But a major-loss claim after a hurricane can accumulate 60 or more attachments. MongoDB has a hard 16 MB size limit per document, but even well below that, a bloated minority of claims slows down every screen that loads them.

The wrong fix is to move all claim documents into a separate collection “just in case,” penalizing the 99% for the 1%. The right fix is what MongoDB’s engineers call the outlier pattern: embed by default, and when a claim crosses a threshold, flip an overflow flag and store the excess in a side collection. The design serves the common case and handles the exception explicitly.

Here’s what that looks like for a hurricane claim. Once the claim crosses the threshold, the application sets the flag and moves the extra documents to the side collection, so the claim record stays small:

The wildfire intake surge

When a database outgrows one server, MongoDB splits it across several, and a field called the shard key decides which server each record lands on. It seems sensible to shard claims by catastrophe (CAT) event code, since the CAT dashboard queries by it. It’s a trap. During an active wildfire, nearly every new claim for days shares one CAT code, so every new claim routes to one server—precisely when intake throughput matters most. Use a hashed shard key on the claim number to spread new claims evenly, and keep the CAT code as an ordinary index for the dashboard.

Both examples carry the same lesson: The data model is where operational resilience is decided, long before the storm arrives.

Three patterns to adopt on day one

Beyond the embed-versus-reference rule, there are three more design patterns to adopt:

  1. Computed totals. Store “total incurred” and “total paid” on the claim rather than re-summing reserves and payments on every read. Claim detail is among the busiest screens in the company; don’t make it do math.

  2. Schema versioning. Stamp every policy and claim with a version number. Insurance records survive for decades under regulatory retention and litigation discovery, and your document shape will change over that time. Without a version marker, that drift becomes an audit problem, not just a technical one. Travelers Insurance(2) is reported to have eliminated a three-day wait for schema changes after moving off a rigid relational model; versioning is what makes that agility safe.

  3. Append-only history. Policy events, claim activity, and increasingly, the step-by-step decision trace of any automated underwriting or fraud-screening agent should only ever be added to, never edited or deleted. In most industries, that’s good hygiene. In insurance, it’s compliance. As regulators turn their attention to AI-driven decisions, an auditable trace of what an automated system decided and why will be the difference between a quick review and a drawn-out one.

What this means for you

None of this requires your engineers to abandon what they know. Multi-document transactions still exist for the moments that need them, such as binding a submission into a policy. The shift is in the starting question. Instead of “What are the entities and how do they relate?” it becomes, “What does the business read and write together, and what changes on its own?”

Keep what’s always read together, well, together. Separate what lives its own life. Plan explicitly for the outlier and the surge. Get those right, and the database finally describes a policy the way your underwriters do.

title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster
summary:
Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms.

When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process:

Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod.

This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. title: The $5 Trillion Shift: Preparing Retail Backends for the Age of AI Agents
summary:
Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant. Instead of a single, stateless chatbot following a rigid script, retailers are building systems where multiple agents collaborate behind the scenes, drawing on preferences and customer purchase history to deliver recommendations that improve with every interaction. More retailers are reconfiguring their backends to reflect the rise in agentic usage, as this is no small trend: McKinsey estimates AI agents could mediate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030.(1)

The need is real, as the race is heating up to quickly respond to customer searches and take service to another level. A customer searching for a pair of running shoes for an upcoming marathon no longer triggers a keyword search. The query kicks off a coordinated reasoning process across multiple specialized agents. This has to happen rapidly and seamlessly to keep consumers' attention and needs met.

The promise of this shift is real, but the real architectural question has nothing to do with which LLM or orchestration framework a team chooses. It has everything to do with where the data lives and whether every agent can see the same version of the truth simultaneously. Increasingly, retailers are finding that solution in MongoDB.

The technology challenge behind multi-agent AI

Building a single AI agent is straightforward with modern LLMs and orchestration frameworks. Building a production multi-agent system is not. Why? Agentic AI has five distinct data needs:

  • Semantic search over vector embeddings 

  • Flexible user context 

  • Conversation state across sessions 

  • Long-term memory that evolves over time 

  • Observability through audit logs

Engineering teams pay a heavy ‘siloed database tax’ to meet these needs, standing up five distinct, single-purpose datastores: a vector store for product discovery, a session store for chat history, a short-term memory store for session context, a long-term memory store for accumulated preferences, and an audit log for compliance and debugging.

That fragmentation comes at a cost. Every additional datastore adds its own SDK, its own operational overhead, and its own failure mode. If the profile agent writes a new preference to one store while the product agent reads from another, the two are only as consistent as the ETL job connecting them. In a real-time conversation, that gap shows up as an agent recommending a product the customer already ruled out, or forgetting a preference captured moments earlier.

Retail makes the problem concrete. Carol asks for running shoes for a road marathon. Her profile has her static preference on file: She wears a size eight. Earlier in this conversation, she mentioned wanting maximum cushioning; that's short-term session context. John asks for running shoes, too. His profile puts him at a size 11, but long-term memory holds something neither his profile nor this conversation does: He needs a waterproof build, a fact learned from a past return after a pair let water soak in. Serving both well, consistently, and across every channel requires holding all three—static preferences, session context, and long-term memory—as one coherent view. This is what we’ve built to make this all happen fluidly

Giving every agent the same context

Retailers building a multi-agent system need specialized agents—including planner agents, profile agents, product agents, and eventually others—to discover and invoke each other's capabilities regardless of which team built them. This is what an open protocol like Agent2Agent (A2A) (2) provides. The Multi Agent Retail Advisor (MARA) is a reference implementation. Here, a planner agent delegates to a profile agent and a product agent, coordinating through A2A. The orchestration framework and LLM are both swappable; MongoDB, the data layer underneath every agent, is not.

Figure 1. Reference architecture for the MARA, showing how the planner, profile, and product agents interact through the A2A protocol, with MongoDB Atlas unifying operational and agentic data via Vector Search, text search, and auto-embeddings.

MongoDB Atlas handles all five agentic data needs natively in one platform, as shown in Figure 2 below. Atlas Vector Search stores product embeddings alongside the catalog data itself, so semantic search runs directly against operational data instead of a separate index to remain in sync. The same flexible document model holds customer context and preferences without a schema migration every time a field changes. Short-term memory lives as a nested array inside each session document, allowing the planner agent to fetch an entire conversation in one read. Long-term memory accumulates in its own collection, capturing facts an agent learns about a customer, like a preference for polyester base layers because they dry faster, independent of any single session. Observability runs through the same platform, too, logging every tool call's inputs, outputs, and latency so a request's full execution path can be reconstructed instantly.

Figure 2. MongoDB Atlas consolidates all single-purpose datastores to meet agentic AI’s data needs into one platform.

For product discovery, retailers build directly on Atlas Vector Search. They embed queries with Voyage AI and match them semantically against the catalog, falling back automatically to Atlas full-text search on the same collection when a query needs it, with no extra infrastructure. Because Voyage AI's newer models share a common embedding space, retailers can embed the catalog once with a larger, accurate model, and then run live queries with a smaller, faster model without ever re-indexing.

A simpler, more resilient stack for IT teams

For retailers, the payoff is architectural simplicity that compounds into speed and cost savings. Teams no longer manage four or five separate systems; they manage one. Schema flexibility, shown in Figure 3, lets agent state and user profiles, each varying by shopper or task, evolve without disruptive migrations. Because MongoDB Atlas scales horizontally, it supports the bursty, unpredictable request patterns of autonomous agents without becoming a bottleneck. Full observability works the same way: A single aggregation pipeline query joins the tool_invocations log, agent_state history, and session record for a request, reconstructing what each agent did, in what order, and how long each step took. That gives IT teams a queryable execution trace for every agent decision, shortening the path from a production issue to a root cause.

Figure 3. Two documents from the agent_state collection and two from the users collection. This shows the same collection, different shape, depending on which agent ran or which shopper it describes.

This consolidation also changes how fast a team can move. The product catalog, user profiles, session history, long-term memory, and tool-invocation logs all live as collections in one MongoDB cluster, not four separate systems linked together. That's the difference between a proof of concept shipping in weeks and one spending its first quarter wiring systems together before a single agent runs.  This setup lowers total cost of ownership the same way: one licensing agreement, one scaling model, and one team. Governance benefits too. Fine-grained access controls, encryption, and audit logging apply consistently across every agent's data, instead of system-by-system configuration. Because the architecture is not tied to a specific framework or model provider, retailers can add new agents, inventory, loyalty, and fulfillment onto the same data plane without replatforming. That matters most for agents no one can name yet. Any future agent built on the same document model plugs into the same unified context, turning what would otherwise be a multi-quarter integration effort into a schema extension.

An experience that feels seamless for customers

For customers, this translates into an experience that feels genuinely continuous. Because every agent reads from and writes to the same unified context, a preference shared in one conversation carries into the next. A question that starts in a chat can hand off cleanly to an inventory agent checking store stock or a loyalty agent applying a reward without the customer repeating themselves. This results in recommendations that get sharper the more a customer interacts with the system and a shopping experience that feels like one relationship rather than a series of disconnected sessions.

Figure 4. Any multi-agent retail architecture needs a swappable layer for orchestration and the LLM, but every agent still needs one constant data layer underneath it. Here, that's MongoDB Atlas beneath MARA's planner, profile, and product agents.

That continuity holds up across channels, not just across conversation turns. A preference a customer states while browsing on mobile is available the next time they open a chat window, walk into a store, or call support because it lives in the same unified profile every agent reads from rather than in a channel-specific cache. Customers also benefit from recommendations that account for their actual history rather than generic popularity signals. This happens since the product agent's semantic search runs against a catalog informed by what a shopper has already bought, browsed, and rejected. For the business, that precision compounds directly into commerce metrics: higher conversion, larger basket sizes, and fewer costly returns from recommendations that miss the mark.

Building for what comes next

The orchestration framework and LLM a retailer chooses today will likely change more than once. What shouldn't change is the data layer holding the system together. MongoDB gives retailers a single, flexible foundation for the knowledge, context, memory, and observability multi-agent retail experiences depend on, so the architecture underneath doesn't have to be rebuilt as frameworks and models evolve. Retailers that consolidate this layer now will be the ones ready to add the next agent—and the next protocol—without starting over.

  1. The automation curve in agentic commerce. McKinsey. January 28th, 2026. https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-automation-curve-in-agentic-commerce

  2. Getting Started with Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol https://codelabs.developers.google.com/intro-a2a-purchasing-concierge#0

title: How Observe.AI Used MongoDB Resharding to Scale Its AI Platform
summary:
Launched in 2017, Observe.AI was originally known for its expertise in conversation intelligence and contact center analytics. In recent years, however, the company has grown into a comprehensive agentic AI platform, and now has three core offerings:

  • AI agents for customers that resolve customer requests across voice and chat.

  • AI agents for frontline teams. These include Observe.AI’s recently launched Companion Agent, which provides human team members real-time guidance and automates work before, during, and after customer interactions.

  • AI agents for operations that evaluate interactions, generate coaching, uncover operational insights, and drive continuous improvement across contact centers.

Observe.AI uses MongoDB Atlas as the foundational data layer for its AI platform and relies on it to store raw customer conversations, AI-generated enrichments, model configurations, and agent metadata.

MongoDB's flexible document model enables rapid iteration as AI models evolve, while its scalability—supporting over 100 clusters and 50+ TB of data—has made it the trusted system of record powering our platform's intelligence layer.

Recently, the team wanted to continue scaling with MongoDB in a way that preserved application availability, reduced operational risk, and created a predictable runway for continued data growth.

The team partnered with MongoDB Consulting’s professional services to scale a production-critical MongoDB Atlas deployment to support Observe.AI’s conversation intelligence platform. The project was a joint engineering effort between Observe.AI and MongoDB that used MongoDB resharding as a practical, online mechanism for redistributing large collections across a broader shard footprint.

Expanding a constrained shard footprint

At the time of the project, the cluster had the following characteristics:

  • A sharded MongoDB Atlas deployment with two data shards plus config servers.

  • Approximately 13 TB of compressed data per data shard, representing roughly 50 TB of uncompressed data overall.

  • Each shard runs on the M140 tier with a disk limit of approximately 14 TB, leaving limited available headroom.

  • A sustained ingest rate of roughly 50 GB per day, making proactive capacity expansion important for safe long-term operations.

  • Several multi-TB collections with significant index footprint and production traffic. This setup had worked at an early stage in the company's cycle, but was no longer fit for purpose and could lead to performance issues or service degradation that would directly impact customers.

The engineering objective of the MongoDB–Observe.AI effort was clear: to expand a constrained shard footprint to a healthier horizontal layout, while also keeping the application online and minimizing disruption to production workloads.

Beyond balancer: a faster redistribution for large-scale data movements

After adding new shard capacity, the team evaluated the default balancer-driven redistribution path. They determined that the balancer was the right tool for ongoing incremental balancing, but the volume of data to be redistributed was large enough that relying on chunk migrations alone would have extended the migration window and kept the original shards under elevated pressure for longer than desired.

The team also tackled a number of other constraints. First, the new shard capacity could receive data, but the pace of redistribution was bounded by balancer and range-deletion throughput; range deletion also created additional background load on shards that were already carrying production traffic. Secondly, existing shards periodically experienced high WiredTiger cache pressure, making it important to avoid prolonged competition between application traffic, balancing, and cleanup activity. Finally, the team wanted a controlled, predictable migration path rather than an extended background redistribution process.

They concluded that the balancer should continue to handle incremental corrections, but a faster and more explicit redistribution mechanism was needed for the initial large-scale data movement.

The four-step resharding plan

Instead of relying solely on balancer migrations, the MongoDB–Observe.AI team designed a controlled resharding plan:

  1. Scale out the cluster

    • Increase capacity by adding multiple new shards (not just one) so that, after redistribution, each shard would hold a manageable share of the ~50 TB dataset.

  2. Prepare the cluster for resharding

    • Ensure no ongoing migrations or resharding jobs.

    • Pin the config servers to remain embedded/dedicated as appropriate for this topology.

    • Disable range deletions and disallow chunk migrations for critical collections so that resharding traffic does not compete with the balancer and range deleter for IOPS.

  3. Run resharding on the largest collections

    • For each large collection (collection6, collection7, collection8, etc.), run reshardCollection to redistribute data across the new shard set, keeping the same shard key but changing the ownership distribution.

    • Execute resharding sequentially per collection to avoid overloading donors, recipients, or the config server.

Table 1. Resharding performance metrics.

4. Clean up and return to normal operations

  • Once data has been redistributed:
    • Remove old empty shards from the cluster.
    • Remove temporary zone configurations that were only needed during the migration.
    • Re‑enable balancing and range deletions for the now‑healthy collections.

Resharding driving greater optimization, performance, and reliability

The joint effort gave Observe.AI a safer and more scalable data foundation for continued platform growth.

Thanks to resharding, the cluster moved from a limited disk runway to a healthier multi-month capacity position, while large multi-TB collections were redistributed across the expanded shard footprint using online resharding rather than relying only on extended balancer-driven chunk migration.

Production reads and writes continued during the clone and catch-up phases, with only the final commit phase requiring a brief write-blocking critical section. The team reduced sustained pressure on the original shards and created more room for future ingest growth, maintenance, and operational flexibility.

Finally, after the migration, the MongoDB balancer returned to its normal role of incremental rebalancing, while the heavy data movement was handled through the more appropriate resharding workflow.

The project highlighted how sharding and resharding can be used proactively as part of ongoing capacity management, helping optimize storage utilization, manage growing data volumes, and maintain platform performance and reliability as workloads scale.

Combining horizontal scale-out and resharding: A winning combo

The key idea behind MongoDB’s resharding capability is simple—sharding should not be the last‑resort, once‑in‑a‑lifetime operation you dread. It should be a practical, fast tool you can use whenever your workload outgrows its current shape.

If you treat sharding as “too expensive” and delay it until your primary is holding tens of TBs, you pay that cost back many times in:

  • Oversized single replica sets,

  • Operational risk,

  • And slow, painful balancing when you finally add shards.

By combining horizontal scale-out with resharding, which has been available since MongoDB 8.0 launched in 2024, you can start small, grow organically, and still have a predictable, efficient path to redistribute data when your cluster—and your business—takes off.

Observe.AI’s  platform processes billions of customer interactions each year, so the infrastructure has to scale as seamlessly as the business. Working alongside the MongoDB team enabled Observe.AI to redistribute more than 50 TB of production data with virtually no disruption to customers. MongoDB 8.0 resharding provided  the operational confidence to expand capacity proactively instead of reacting to infrastructure limits, allowing Observe.AI’s engineering teams to stay focused on delivering innovation for customers.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications
summary:
We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm.

This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts.

What is the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context.

Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember context.

What types of memory does an AI application need?

An AI application needs five kinds of memory, each kept for a different length of time and retrieved differently. This integration automatically categorizes each type of memory and stores it in MongoDB Atlas; here are short definitions of the five memory types:

  • Session: The conversation an application or agent has in each session. This helps the application follow what the user just said.

  • Semantic: Facts about people, entities, and preferences, so users don't have to repeat themselves.

  • Procedural: Workflows and instructions, so the application carries out tasks the way you've defined them.

  • Episodic: Key events and outcomes, so the application can recall what happened before. Kept for one year of inactivity by default.

  • Scratchpad: Temporary notes for work in progress. They expire after an hour and can be promoted to episodic memory if they turn out to matter.

Semantic and procedural memories are versioned, so history is preserved when a fact changes. The semantic, procedural, and episodic tiers use MongoDB Vector Search, which finds stored memories by semantic meaning rather than by exact keywords.

This integration automatically creates the vector indexes and detects embedding dimensions at startup. Developers can use any AI SDK embedding model to create vector indexes, including Voyage AI, OpenAI, Cohere, or Google.

Figure 1. How the integration works with MongoDB Atlas and the Vercel SDK interface.

How should memory age?

Each category of memory has its own retention policy, so short-lived notes expire quickly, and long-term facts are stored for longer. The MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration ships with defaults for every category, which developers can customize if they desire.

Effective memory retention requires a balance. Keeping memories indefinitely can decrease retrieval performance and increase costs, while deleting them too early can cause applications to forget important context. This integration includes features to help developers easily set the right balance:

  • Retention modes: Choose none (never expire), ttl (expire after a set time), ttl+importance (expire after a set time unless the memory is marked important), or dynamic, where you define your own forgetting time period.
  • Model-driven forgetting: With memory_forget, the model can delete a specific memory when a user says "forget that." Removal usually happens within about 60 seconds.

Because the memory is stored in MongoDB Atlas, application operational data, its memory, and the vector search that retrieves it run on one platform. Developers can secure, monitor, and scale a single database without bolting on a separate vector store or memory service alongside it.

What changes when you run the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration in production?

This production release gives developers greater controls over their data and flexibility in how they use the integration:

  • Reliable session history: By default, the model decides when to save and read conversation turns, so it can occasionally skip one. For production, you can use the AI SDK hooks so that the application’s own code loads and saves the transcript at every turn. Every user, assistant, and tool message is saved exactly once.

  • Separate data per customer: Developers can add a filter field, such as tenant_id, to the application’s vector indexes to limit each search to a single customer's memories.

  • Application names and layout: Developers can rename collections and indexes to match the existing application schema or turn off indexing for unused categories. 

  • Open source: The package is licensed under Apache 2.0 and works with any AI SDK model.

Get started today

Developers can add memory to an existing Vercel AI SDK project in three steps. This integration works with AI SDK v6 and v7 and requires a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

  1. Install the package and its peer dependencies: npm install @mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory ai mongodb

  2. Create a memory instance with an Atlas connection string and an embedding model.

  3. Pass the memory tools to the application, scoped to a user and session.

From there, the model decides when to save and when to search for memories.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents
summary:
The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore.

Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027).

What is the Claude Agent SessionStore?

But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store.

That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn.

That is the gap the MongoDB Session Adapter closes.

This is especially useful for enterprises that have multiple teams developing agents across many machines, who need session storage that survives host failures, scales as the agent fleet increases, and enforces the same access controls and retention rules as the rest of their data estate, not a bolt-on system built solely for agent memory.

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter gives Claude agents durable session storage: a record of the conversation and its action history that lets an agent pick back up exactly where it left off, whether that's on the same laptop, a different server, or any server in a distributed deployment.

The adapter helps cover three crucial areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: Whether a different backend instance picks up a conversation after a restart or a user resumes on a different device, session state doesn't live on the machine that started it. Because every step is mirrored to MongoDB as it happens, any instance in your deployment can resume exactly where the last one left off.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container gets rescheduled mid-conversation, nothing is lost. Entries are written to MongoDB as they occur, not batched or cached locally, so whichever instance picks the session back up sees the same state as the failed one, up to the last completed step.

  • Retention and auditability: Many teams need to retain agent transcripts to meet internal data-retention or audit requirements. Instead of standing up a separate system just for that, session data lives in the MongoDB cluster you're already operating, under the same access controls and backup policies as the rest of your data.

As agents move from prototypes to real-world applications, they need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over a long time. However, developers still need to build their own tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state.

What is the Google ADK?

The Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

Google ADK offers developers an extensive set of tools for creating, deploying, assessing, and scaling agents, enabling developers to build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows.

How does the MongoDB Google ADK Integration help?

Developers can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. With MongoDB as the data layer, developers can keep the data their agents search over, the conversation state that needs to survive a restart or a scaled-out instance, and the memories agents build over time, all in the same place as the rest of their application data. That means no separate database to stand up for retrieval, no pipeline syncing app data into a different memory index, and no added latency pulling context from another system before the agent can respond.

ADK supplies the agent framework and tool interface; this integration provides the data and persistence layer beneath it, so developers can easily take an agent from prototype to production. These agents can maintain conversation and session memory independent of any single machine, and carry a user's history across sessions.

Providing a unified agent architecture

At the core of this integration is Google ADK 2.0, which serves as the code-first orchestration layer for multi-agent systems. ADK 2.0 provides the deployment framework, while MongoDB provides session and memory storage for agents.

Integrating directly with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, ADK 2.0 eliminates the need for custom routing logic by providing standardized tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry, and enterprise access controls out of the box.
